introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Les pertes territoriales et de population sont données de manière approximative (« environ 13 % du territoire », « environ 10 % de la population ») ; aucune citation attribuée.

questions.enonce_markdown:
"A harsh, unfair and unjust treaty." Is this a fair description of the Treaty of Versailles of 1919?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 between Germany and the Allies, at the end of the Paris Peace Conference. Germans called it a *Diktat* (dictated peace) and many people outside Germany, such as the economist J. M. Keynes, called it too harsh. This essay examines the three adjectives in the quotation: whether the treaty was harsh, unfair and unjust, and concludes that it was certainly harsh, in some respects unfair, but that the claim of injustice is too simple.

**1. The terms of the treaty.**
- *War guilt.* Article 231 made Germany and her allies responsible for the loss and damage caused by the war, which was the basis for reparations.
- *Reparations.* Germany had to pay compensation to the Allies; in 1921 the total was fixed at 132 billion gold marks.
- *Territory.* Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine to France, Eupen and Malmedy to Belgium, North Schleswig to Denmark (after a plebiscite), a large part of Posen and West Prussia to Poland (the Polish Corridor, with Danzig as a free city), the Saar was placed under the League of Nations for fifteen years, and all colonies were taken as mandates. Germany lost about 13 per cent of its European territory and about 10 per cent of its population.
- *Military.* The army was limited to 100,000 men without conscription, the navy was limited and could not have submarines, there was no air force or tanks, and the Rhineland was demilitarised and occupied by Allied troops for up to fifteen years. Union with Austria was forbidden.

**2. Arguments that the treaty was harsh, unfair and unjust.**
- Germany was not invited to the negotiations and was forced to sign under the threat of renewed blockade and war, which is why it was called a *Diktat*.
- The "war guilt" clause was resented because many Germans did not accept that Germany alone was responsible for the war.
- The reparations were seen as impossible to pay, and the loss of territory and economic resources (coal in the Saar and Silesia, iron ore in Lorraine) hindered recovery. The treaty contributed to the hyperinflation of 1923 and to bitterness which the Nazis later exploited.
- It was said to violate the principle of self-determination in the Fourteen Points of President Wilson, which Germany believed would be the basis of peace: Germans in Poland, Czechoslovakia (the Sudetenland) and Austria were not allowed to choose, and the union with Austria was forbidden.
- The disarmament was one-sided, since the other powers did not disarm as promised.

**3. Arguments that it was not unfair or unjust.**
- Germany had treated Russia far more harshly in the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918), taking a very large part of its population and industry, which shows how Germany would have behaved as a victor.
- Germany had invaded Belgium and France, and the war devastated northern France; the demand for compensation was therefore not unreasonable, and the Allies had suffered huge losses.
- Germany remained united and a great power, with a large population and a strong industrial base; it had not been divided or occupied, and the actual reparations were reduced (Dawes Plan 1924, Young Plan 1929, and in 1932 the Lausanne agreement effectively ended them).
- The treaty was a compromise: Clemenceau wanted much more (for example, a separate Rhineland), while Wilson and Lloyd George wanted a more moderate settlement. In many cases the changes in territory followed the principle of nationality, as in the return of Alsace-Lorraine and the restoration of Poland.

**4. Assessment.** The treaty was harsh in the demands which it made of a defeated nation, and some of its terms (the war guilt clause, the way it was imposed, the limits on self-determination) were unfair or at least badly handled. But its terms were not as severe as Germany's own proposals or as the aims of some Allies, and it was a compromise that satisfied no one: too harsh to conciliate Germany, too weak to prevent its recovery. It is therefore a fair description only in part.

**Conclusion.** The description "harsh, unfair and unjust" is partly fair. The treaty was harsh and in several respects unfair, particularly in the way it was imposed and the war guilt clause, but it was not as unjust as German propaganda claimed, and it was less severe than other treaties of the time. Its greatest weakness was that it left Germany resentful but strong enough to challenge it.
